Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
# Before the City Wakes

Before the street wakes, there is a brief interval when the city belongs to no one. Delivery trucks have not yet filled the curb with noise. Shop shutters remain gray, and windows hold the reflection of a sky that is still deciding whether it will be clear. Somewhere, a bus exhales at the depot. Somewhere else, a kettle clicks off. These small signals mark the beginning of a day that will soon become crowded with errands, obligations, and urgent opinions.

I used to think mornings began with alarm clocks. Now I know they begin earlier, in the quiet struggle between sleep and awareness. The body wakes slowly, like a lamp warming in a cold room. Ideas arrive in fragments: an unfinished sentence, a forgotten name, the melody of a song heard years ago. For several minutes, the mind drifts without demanding a destination. Then the world taps on the glass, and practical life returns with lists. Outside, birds test the branches, a broom scrapes a courtyard, and the first bicycle bell rings with impossible confidence. Every morning offers this invitation.

Breakfast has become my daily negotiation with time. Coffee suggests patience. Toast suggests efficiency. A banana eaten while reading leaves crumbs among the pages and creates the illusion that both hunger and knowledge can be managed. I sit at the small table beside the window and watch ordinary people pass. A gardener ties his apron. Two students compare notes under a young tree. A woman carrying flowers chooses the longer route, perhaps because she has nowhere else to be. She moves as though the morning has granted her a secret that the rest of us have not yet earned today.

Not long ago, I believed productivity was a moral virtue. An empty calendar felt like failure, and rest required a justification strong enough to withstand questioning. I answered messages before brushing my teeth, filled quiet hours with useful tasks, and mistook motion for meaning. This was easier than admitting that I did not know what I wanted. It was easier to become useful than curious, because usefulness could be measured. Today, attention is becoming the foundation beneath my ambition. It reminds me that noticing the birds outside does not prevent hard work, but it may make the work more careful.

The work itself has changed because I have changed. I no longer ask only what can be finished, but what deserves to be done. There is a difference between the task that fills an hour and the task that gives an hour meaning. Writing a careful letter may produce no visible result, yet it can repair something distant. Reading twenty pages slowly may alter the architecture of a thought. A walk without an audio program can return a memory intact. Perhaps this is why my best plans now begin with one protected patch of stillness before the world makes requests.

Even so, I cannot romanticize slowness. Some days demand immediate action. A pipe bursts. A deadline approaches. A friend needs help. There are mornings when the city has barely opened and already feels too full, when every message carries a small weight and every decision removes another option. On those mornings, my quiet interval feels less like a gift and more like a narrowing window. I hurry to the bus, drink coffee standing, and speak in clipped sentences. The day does not care that I would prefer to move gently through it. Yet even hurried days contain unexpected kindnesses nearby.

Usually they arrive through strangers. A driver waits while an older woman loads groceries. Someone holds a door with a backpack full of books. A cashier remembers that I always choose mint tea and asks whether I am having a good morning. These gestures take seconds, yet they interrupt the story I am telling myself about the world. Strangers remind us that no life is merely a transaction, though most cities are built as if it were. I try to carry that reminder home. Perhaps recognition is citizenship, a way of saying that we all belong to one another here.

By noon, the city I loved in the early quiet has become difficult to see. Sidewalks are crowded, traffic folds into a metal river, and everyone seems to know exactly where they are going. I used to envy that certainty. Now I suspect it is partly costume. Behind the fixed expression is a person choosing breakfast, avoiding a call, worrying about a parent, or looking for a shade tree. We perform confidence because the alternative would be to stand exposed before the pace of the street. Still, their momentum perhaps carries me forward more often than it harms me today.

Afternoon arrives with a change in light. Buildings cast longer shadows, glass turns copper, and the day’s sharp edges begin to soften. I eat lunch without a screen. The food tastes clearer, though perhaps that is only because I am paying attention. Then I walk toward the river, following a route with no purpose beyond movement. Willows trail their fingers in the water. A rowing team passes in perfect formation, each oar dipping and rising like wings. I remember how, as a child, I believed the river carried every unanswered question away. Some questions returned, but in entirely different forms.

Evening gathers the day into fewer, larger shapes. The errands are done or abandoned. The messages are answered or allowed to wait. At dinner, conversation moves slowly because no one wants to leave the table too soon. I listen to the refrigerator hum and the pipes settle inside the walls. Outside, the sky releases the last blue of evening. The city is not sleeping yet, but it has softened, making room for whatever comes next. Perhaps this is enough: to have seen the morning, felt the noon, and preserved a small amount of wonder throughout the entire day without fear.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical first-person reflection turns ordinary details of a city day into an argument for attention over compulsive productivity.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gentle and observant, moving from quiet sensory details toward a modest moral claim: noticing the world can make work and relationships more careful, not less important. Its pathos comes from the speaker’s admission that usefulness once felt easier than curiosity, alongside the pressure of deadlines and crowded days. The reader is invited to notice small acts and moments of stillness without romanticizing an escape from responsibility.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds the daily rhythm of a city—kettles, buses, breakfast, strangers’ gestures, river light—and repeatedly links these details to attention, rest, and belonging. It favors an ethic of measured work and ordinary kindness, while acknowledging that some days allow little room for slowness.

## Evidence line
> Today, attention is becoming the foundation beneath my ambition.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The essay coherently returns to attention and ordinary kindness across the day, though its reflective, polished style relies on familiar lyrical motifs.
